**当前摘要**（在 `sections/abstract.tex`）：
```
Do hidden states outperform text for detecting unsafe reasoning in chain-of-thought models? We show that the answer reverses depending on which transformer layer the probe reads, a choice most studies treat as trivial. Studying commitment-point detection across four self-jailbreaking reasoning models (two architectures, two scales), we find that crossing-rate metrics systematically select shallow layers (L0--L10) while threshold-based metrics select deep layers (L14--L63), a divergence of 14 to 61 layers. At shallow layers the two modalities perform equivalently; at deep layers hidden-state probes gain +20--22pp precision, cross-validated at 7--8B. The mechanism is cosine compression: shallow-layer representations compress directional information, inflating frequency-based metrics near the noise floor. This bias generalizes across models and a second dataset (AdvBench); the geometric precondition (cosine compression) extends to a fifth architecture (Gemma-2). The hidden-state advantage is conditional: it diminishes with stronger text encoders and remains only suggestive at 32B due to small samples. Seven alternative detection methods all fail to match supervised probing. Layer selection metric is a critical, overlooked specification choice in safety probing studies.
```

tool_args.new_string: Reasoning models can self-jailbreak: their chain of thought transitions from safe to harmful content without adversarial input. Detecting when this shift occurs (the commitment point) requires real-time monitoring, and hidden-state probes offer a direct window into the model's internal reasoning. Yet which transformer layer to read is routinely treated as an implementation detail. We show this choice matters. Across four models (two architectures, two scales), crossing-rate metrics systematically select shallow layers (L0--L10) while threshold-based metrics select deep layers (L14--L63), a divergence of 14 to 61 layers. This gap reverses whether hidden states outperform text: at deep layers, hidden-state probes gain +20--22\,pp precision over text (cross-validated at 7--8B); at shallow layers, the two modalities perform equivalently. The mechanism is cosine compression: shallow representations compress directional information, inflating frequency-based metrics near the noise floor. This bias generalizes across models and a second dataset (AdvBench), and the geometric precondition extends to a fifth architecture (Gemma-2). The advantage diminishes with stronger text encoders and remains suggestive at 32B; seven alternative detection methods fail to match supervised probing. Layer selection metric is a critical, overlooked specification choice in safety probing studies.\footnote{Code and data: \url{https://anonymous.4open.science/r/contrastive_trace_safety-A178/}.}
